newsitem.title: JAPAN: Asia Metals -- Concerns grow over Ok Tedi mine.
newsitem.headline: Asia Metals -- Concerns grow over Ok Tedi mine.

text.p: Concerns are growing in Japan over the Ok Tedi copper and gold mine in Papua New Guinea, which remains closed due to dry weather, base metal traders said on Wednesday.
"We don't expect much impact from strikes at Inco (Ltd). But we're worried over the Ok Tedi mine," said a copper trader.
Traders said if the dry weather continued, forcing the Ok Tedi mine to declare force majeure, domestic smelters would need to fill the gap on the spot market.
So far, Japanese smelters have brushed aside such worries, saying imports of copper concentrates from Ok Tedi account for less than 10 percent of Japan's total supplies.
On Wednesday, Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd said it would further scale back operations at the Ok Tedi mine unless there was significant rain by the end of this week.
June deliveries of copper concentrate to Japan have been delayed due to low water levels on the Fly River.
Traders said the Japanese physical copper market remained quiet with premiums unchanged at $60-70 per tonne as users cut back their stocks ahead of summer holidays in July and August.
In the aluminium market, premiums remained high at $88 to $93 per tonne for deliveries in the third quarter, traders said, though not many deals were struck as few were willing to sell.
"There's nothing you can do if you don't have enough metal now," said one trader at a foreign trading house. "It's also difficult to buy distant months as nearbys are expensive."

Though traders agreed that demand from the car, construction and beverage industry had cooled down after overheating earlier this year, some doubted whether there would be as much decline in the second half of this year as was earlier expected.

"Domestic demand will fall this year. But if the decline is not as large as people had forecast, premiums will remain high as many will be forced to purchase the metal on the spot market," the trader said.
Japanese premiums for zinc were barely changed at $40 to $50 per tonne despite continued exports from China, traders said.
"The market has been quiet apart from some exports from China," said one trader. "Though domestic demand is likely to drop later this year, exports seem to be faring quite well."
Asked about the dollar's latest decline against the yen, the trader said: "I'm not worried. But if it falls through 100 yen, that's a different story."

In the latest key economic data, the Ministry of International Trade and Industry said on Monday that crude steel production in the third quarter would remain flat against an estimated output of 26.05 million tonnes in the second quarter.
The steel output in the April-June quarter climbed 7.6 percent from a-year-earlier period, mainly due to increased demand from the car industry and the housing sector, it said.
